paper.title: Penning ionization of He(2^3S) + Ar
paper.affiliation: Materials and Molecular Research Division and Department of Chemistry, Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720
paper.funding: U. S. Energy Research and Development Administration

research.context: Penning ionization of He(2^3S) + Ar is a prototype system. Three quantities needed for complete description: Vo (real interaction potential), Vi (imaginary part for ionization), V+ (ionic potential for HeAr+). Previous potentials (e.g., Olson's) with Vi from Illenberger/Niehaus or Pesnelle et al. gave good total cross sections but failed for differential cross sections. Hickman and Morgner (1976) derived a Morse form for Vo with accurate well but uncertain wall steepness.
goals: Measure differential cross sections at 65 and 132 meV with reduced uncertainties.
Determine Vo and Vi that fit both differential and total ionization cross sections.
Critically examine the first-order semiclassical approximation for phase shifts.
Establish guidelines for validity of the semiclassical approach.
research.process: Penning ionization: He(2^3S) + Ar → He + Ar^+ + e^-

states.final: He(1^1S) + Ar^+ + e^- (Penning ionization), possibly HeAr^+ (associative ionization)
states.quenched: He(2^1S) quenched by helical pyrex He resonance lamp

methods: First-order semiclassical approximation for complex phase shifts (Eqs. 2-3)
Quantum mechanical close-coupling (Numerov algorithm) for exact phase shifts
Partial wave expansion for differential and total cross sections (Eqs. 7-8)

potential_forms.Vo: MMSV (modified Morse spline van der Waals) piecewise: Morse-like inner, cubic spline intermediate, -C6/r^6 - C8/r^8 long-range (Eq. 1)
potential_forms.V+: Not determined in this work; inferred from Penning electron energy distributions and Penning/associative ionization ratio

approximations: Vi << Vo (perturbative treatment of imaginary part)
Vi independent of collision energy (assumed, but high-energy data suggest weak energy dependence)
Semiclassical trajectory determined solely by Vo

numerical.integration_method: Numerov algorithm for quantum mechanical phase shifts

differential_cross_section.measurement_details: Average of 8 scans at 65 meV, 3 scans at 132 meV; counting time 45 sec per angle; He beam velocity spread 6–8% FWHM, Ar beam 6–8% FWHM

results.potential: MMSV Vo with ε=0.1 kcal/mole, rm=5.5 Å, β1=5.2 fits small-angle DCS at both energies; exponential Vi with B=5.2934 Å^-1, Ro=3.55 Å fits large-angle DCS and total ionization cross section of Illenberger and Niehaus.
results.semiclassical_validity: First-order semiclassical approximation for real phase shift holds when opacity < 0.8. For Vi increased by factor 5, opacities exceed 0.95 and approximation breaks down (Fig. 7). Quantum mechanically, only large-angle DCS affected by increased Vi; small-angle oscillations unchanged.
results.trade_offs: β1 (repulsive wall slope) and Vi are correlated: different (β1, Vi) pairs yield identical DCS at a single energy but different total cross section energy dependence (Fig. 5). Vi parametrization ambiguity (changing Ro vs B) also resolved only by total cross section energy dependence.
results.energy_dependence: High-energy data (132 meV) prefer smaller Vi than 65 meV; total cross section easier to fit if Vi decreases weakly with energy, but uncertainties prevent firm conclusion.
results.literature_discrepancy: Pesnelle et al. and Illenberger/Niehaus total cross sections agree at low energies but diverge at high energies; authors favor Illenberger data which agree with their calculations.

figures.Fig. 1: Lab angular distribution of elastically scattered He(2^3S) from Ar at 65 meV (a) and 132 meV (b). Solid curves: calculated DCS using optical potential from this work.
figures.Fig. 2: MMSV potential (solid), imaginary part Vi (dash-dot), Olson's Vo (dashed). Dotted portion indicates region not accessed experimentally.
figures.Fig. 3: Comparison of calculated DCS using this work's optical potential (solid) vs Olson's potential with Illenberger's coupling (dashed).
figures.Fig. 4: Total ionization cross section vs relative velocity: calculated (solid) vs Illenberger and Niehaus data (circles).
figures.Fig. 5: (a) DCS at 65 meV for two optical potentials: β1=5.2, Vi=exp[-5.2934(r-3.55)] (solid) and β1=4.5, Vi=exp[-5.2934(r-3.35)] (dashed) – indistinguishable. (b) Corresponding total cross sections vs velocity: solid agrees with Illenberger/Niehaus, dashed does not.
figures.Fig. 6: Phase shift difference Δη^R = |η^R(Vo) - η^R(Vo-iVi)| vs opacity (1 - exp(-4η^I)) for Vo, Vo-iVi, Vo-i10Vi, Vo-i100Vi. Quantum mechanical (Numerov). Shows Δη^R small for opacity < 0.8.
figures.Fig. 7: Calculated DCS for Vi_opt and 5Vi_opt comparing semiclassical (approx) vs quantum mechanical (exact). For Vi_opt, both agree; for 5Vi_opt, semiclassical fails at large angles.

equations.Eq. 1: MMSV potential piecewise definition: f(x)=exp[-2β1(x-1)]-2exp[-β1(x-1)] for x<x1; f(x)=exp[-2β2(x-1)]-2exp[-β2(x-1)] for x1<x<x2; f(x)=b1+(x-x2){b2+(x-x3)[b3+(x-x2)b4]} for x2<x<x3; f(x)=-C6 x^-6 - C8 x^-8 for x>x3, where x=r/rm.
equations.Eq. 2: Semiclassical complex phase shift: η_l = η_l^R + iη_l^I = (1/ħ) ∫_{r_c}^∞ [2μ(E - V)]^{1/2} - l(l+1)ħ^2/(2μ r^2) dr - k r_c + π(l+1)/2, with V = Vo - iVi, r_c complex turning point.
equations.Eq. 3: First-order expansion: η_l^R ≈ (1/ħ) ∫_{r_c}^∞ [2μ(E - Vo) - l(l+1)ħ^2/r^2]^{1/2} dr - k r_c + π(l+1)/2; η_l^I ≈ -(1/ħ) ∫_{r_c}^∞ Vi / [2μ(E - Vo) - l(l+1)ħ^2/r^2]^{1/2} dr.
equations.Eq. 4: Opacity function: PI = 1 - exp(-4η_l^I) = 1 - exp[-4 ∫ (η_l^I(r)) dr].
equations.Eq. 5: Radial velocity: v_l(r) = [2/μ (E - V_eff(r))]^{1/2}, with V_eff = Vo + l(l+1)ħ^2/(2μ r^2).
equations.Eq. 7: Total inelastic cross section: σ_inel = (π/k^2) Σ_{l} (2l+1) PI.
equations.Eq. 8: Differential cross section: dσ/dΩ = |Σ_{l} (2l+1)[1 - exp(2iη_l)] P_l(cos θ)|^2 (standard partial wave expansion).

limitations: Trade-off between β1 and Vi: DCS at single energy cannot uniquely determine both; need total cross section energy dependence.
Vi parametrization ambiguity: changing Ro vs B yields same DCS at one energy but different energy dependence.
Assumption of energy-independent Vi; high-energy data suggest weak energy dependence but uncertainties are large.
Semiclassical approximation valid only for opacity < 0.8 (Vi not too large).
Controversy in high-energy total ionization cross section measurements between Pesnelle et al. and Illenberger/Niehaus.
Limited energy range (only two collision energies) for differential cross sections.
High-energy (132 meV) data have larger uncertainties.
Vi form assumed exponential; may not hold at very small r (e.g., leveling off as r→0).
